name: Pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium)
short: Deaths: an infant given mint tea brewed from plants containing pennyroyal oil (liver failure); 1 of 4 people who swallowed pennyroyal. Used to cause abortion. Leaf-extract trial: no adverse effects.
text: This entry covers pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium) taken by mouth. The page product is a standardized leaf extract made with 70% aqueous ethanol; most reports of harm concern pennyroyal oil or teas, and the form is given for each source. Leaf extract: in a 2-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 100 people with functional dyspepsia who were also taking famotidine (50 on the extract), the extract did not significantly affect blood counts or liver and kidney tests, and the patients did not experience any adverse drug effect; the abstract does not report the extract's pulegone or menthofuran content. Infants (tea brewed from plants containing the oil): two infants given home-brewed mint tea, whose plants were found to contain pennyroyal oil, developed liver and nerve injury; one died of fulminant liver failure with brain swelling and necrosis, and the other developed liver dysfunction and a severe epileptic encephalopathy. The authors say such mint teas are mistakenly used as home remedies for minor ailments and colic in infants. Other case reports: a case series of four people who swallowed pennyroyal (the abstract does not give the form taken) reports one death, and its review of 18 earlier case reports documented moderate to severe toxicity in people exposed to at least 10 mL of pennyroyal oil; the authors call pennyroyal's liver toxicity potentially lethal. Four more records have no abstract and are known only by their titles: 'Pennyroyal poisoning: a fatal case', 'Pennyroyal oil ingestion: report of a case', 'Pennyroyal oil poisoning and hepatotoxicity', and a report of liver failure from pennyroyal tea interacting with medicines broken down by cytochrome P450 enzymes. A 2024 review says pennyroyal herbal teas are not recommended because of liver toxicity, that infants and children can die if they consume it, and that the essential oil should never be taken internally because even small doses can be fatal; it reports that toxicological studies found low doses of the plant's extracts not toxic and its essential oils extremely toxic, without saying what dose counts as low. A review of plant-related seizures lists pennyroyal among 11 plants whose essential oils are powerful convulsants (its own three cases are not said to involve pennyroyal). Pregnancy: pennyroyal has long been used to try to cause abortion, and a 2023 review lists it among herbal abortifacients with significant illness and death. A poison-centre survey in Montevideo of 86 cases of herbal infusions taken to cause abortion describes an over-the-counter herbal product whose four listed components include pennyroyal, and reports multiple organ failure in some people who took it and one death after it; the product name, which links these outcomes, is not repeated here, the outcomes belong to the four-herb product rather than to pennyroyal alone, and self-inflicted instrumental manipulation was found in 4 of the patients with multiple organ failure and in one of those who died (the abstract does not say which products those patients took). In pregnant rats, pennyroyal extracts disrupted the uterus and placenta or ended the pregnancy (an animal study). A letter with no abstract is titled 'Pregnancy unaffected by pennyroyal usage'; its title gives no form, dose or number of people. Blood pressure: a review lists pennyroyal oil among herbal products that may cause high blood pressure (oil, not the leaf extract). Interactions: the only interaction record found is the title-only report on medicines broken down by cytochrome P450 enzymes; no other interaction data were found in the cited sources.
